plos-pone-0004827: In type 1 diabetes, surviving beta cells might regenerate if given the right signal. Pechhold and colleagues show blood glucose levels regulate beta-cell proliferation in diabetic mice. The finding links metabolism to regeneration. Sugar as a growth signal for insulin makers.
plos-pone-0005427: HIV scrambles B-cell memory, yet some cells keep producing refined antibodies. Cagigi and colleagues show CD27-negative B cells produce class-switched, hypermutated antibodies during chronic HIV infection. The finding revises B-cell biology. Resilience in the antibody factory under chronic viral siege.
plos-pone-0005527: Visual cortex areas V2 and V3 were thought to need V1 input. Schmid and colleagues lesioned V1 and still found visually driven activation in macaque V2/V3. The bypass pathways reveal parallel visual routes. Vision without the primary gateway, mapped in monkeys.
plos-pone-0005627: Germs can brew useful diols from simple starting bits. Xiao and team studied acetoin breakdown and acetylbutanediol making in Bacillus pumilus. The energy paths allow green reactions. Germ makers for factory-made diols, tuned in set media, with biotech routes to earth-kind goods.
plos-pone-0005727: Misshapen proteins clump in nerve-wasting ill. Kvam and team aimed fibrous glutamine repeats shapes in live cells, raising clumping and harm. The work probes disease path steps. Shape as a drug target in live cells, Huntington's and Machado-Joseph biology, across alpha-synuclein and huntingtin shapes.
plos-pone-0005827: Head pain burden Pakistan's group heavily. Murtaza and team sorted headache troubles from Pakistan medical data. The looking back review maps how common. Migraine and tension-type, counted in the clinic, the forty-six percent how common context, public health's missed problem, medical data from Pakistan, ill tracking telling care.
plos-pone-0006427: Drug tests need cheap binders. Qi and team fished anti-sulfadimidine antibody bits from cells via ribosome display. The bits spot drug traces in food — tiny detectors for drug leftovers, built, on a low-cost platform. Food safety's helper, with single-chain bits picked from lab cells as source.
plos-pone-0006527: Sugar illness starves its own peacekeepers. Jailwala and team found IL-2 shortage drives calmer T cell death in type 1 sugar illness. The guards die unfed — immunity's friendly fire, mapped, with FOXP3 cells in focus. Beta cells attacked, in self-attack disease: calm lost.
plos-pone-0006627: Modeling malaria prevention for kids. Águas and team modeled spaced shield treatment's malaria toll in infants and children. The sims weigh IPTi and IPTc — malaria's virtual trial, run, in sub-Saharan Africa. Life-threatening illness, sickness rate: new plans, disease burden, burden tackled.
plos-pone-0009427: Prostate cancer often begins as small abnormal growths called PIN, and the MYC gene is a prime suspect. In engineered mice, the researchers pinpoint exactly when and in which prostate cells MYC switches on to trigger these precancerous lesions. The study maps cancer's opening moves in the prostate, giving scientists a precise model for testing early interventions.
plos-pone-0009527: India carries a heavy burden of drug-resistant tuberculosis, yet data on the most resistant forms — XDR-TB — remains scarce. This hospital study identifies the risk factors behind multidrug- and extensively drug-resistant TB. The findings give public health officials concrete targets for catching resistant TB earlier.
plos-pone-0009627: Hepatitis C might be attacked with RNA enzymes — ribozymes — designed to cut the virus's genetic material. This study investigates a new generation of these molecular scissors. The paper explores a high-potential weapon against a virus that infects millions. If the approach works, it could give doctors a precision tool that strikes only the virus.
plos-pone-0010427: An optical trap plus a laser spectrometer can read a single living blood cell's chemistry. This study applies Raman tweezers to individual red and white cells. The paper demonstrates chemistry at the single-cell level. The technique opens a window into blood chemistry one cell at a time.
plos-pone-0010527: Starting HIV treatment can unmask TB — and that TB may blunt immune recovery. This large African clinic study measures the effect. The paper quantifies a cruel interaction of two epidemics colliding in one patient. The numbers argue for TB screening at the start of HIV therapy.
plos-pone-0010627: ALS kills motor neurons — and the damage may spread like an infection. This study shows SOD1 fibrils from mouse spinal cord can seed new fibrils. The paper supports a propagative mechanism for ALS. The seeding suggests ALS spreads cell to cell like a prion.
plos-pone-0010727: Biochemists need exact numbers on how enzymes behave. This study presents a computer-run automated assay that measures enzyme kinetic parameters across conditions. The paper delivers a lab workhorse. The automation lets one machine do the work of many hands. The tool speeds up drug and enzyme research.
plos-pone-0010827: Genetic studies often have holes in their data. This study compares methods that fill gaps by imputing untyped genotypes for association testing. The paper benchmarks the approaches. The comparison guides stronger gene-hunting studies. The winner sharpens the hunt for disease genes.
plos-pone-0010927: The chytrid fungus is driving amphibians extinct. This study measures how chytrid-caused death varies within and between populations of the midwife toad. The paper reveals uneven vulnerability. The finding helps target conservation where it counts. The variation may hold the key to survival.
plos-pone-0011027: Can strangers judge a face's mate appeal? This study tests whether people in the Bolivian Amazon can assess facial cues linked to sexual selection. The paper probes a universal cognitive skill. The finding connects faces to evolution. The skill may be written in our genes.
plos-pone-0011127: Even at Pompeii's edges, the volcanic surge killed with heat. This study documents lethal thermal impact at the periphery of pyroclastic surges. The paper reconstructs how victims died. The finding informs volcanic-hazard science. The heat reconstruction honors the victims' story.
plos-pone-0011227: Gambian children discharged after severe anemia often fall ill again. This study tests preventive drug treatment to stop anemia recurrence after hospital discharge. The paper offers a protection strategy. The finding could save young lives. The saved lives justify the intervention.
plos-pone-0011327: A human protein helps the chickenpox virus break in. This study shows insulin-degrading enzyme reshapes varicella-zoster virus gE, boosting infectivity and stability. The paper reveals a viral trick. The finding aids virology. The aided virology blocks the helper. The blocked helper stops the virus.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1227:
A second Sato report to Togo bears the date 19 July 1945. Two cables in a day from the Moscow embassy show the pace of the exchange. Tokyo wanted news; Sato had mostly warnings to send.

The envoy's problem was plain: the Soviet side gained by waiting. Each day of delay weakened Japan and strengthened Moscow's hand for the war's end. Sato's reports pressed Tokyo to face that truth and to sharpen its terms. This cable is one more turn of that screw. It is part of the secret record the Potsdam leaders read while they drafted Japan's surrender terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1327:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of State on 17 July 1945, the summit's opening day. Grew's home office began its Potsdam circuit with this message. The circuit would run daily until the team came home.

Opening-day cables set the pattern: what Washington sent, how fast, and in what tone. The department's chief abroad needed the capital's news to bargain well. This note starts that flow in the record. It is a small, early piece of the two-ended machine that ran American foreign policy through the most crowded weeks of 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1427:
The British delegation submitted a text at Potsdam on 30 July 1945. By that date Attlee had replaced Churchill, and the British team was finishing the talks under new leadership. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

A text tabled in the summit's last days speaks to the drafting of the closing bargain. The British side, wedged between American wealth and Soviet numbers, used careful drafting as its lever. Readers can weigh this late British text against the protocol signed two days later. It shows the delegation still working its points to the end, under a prime minister who had held the job for less than a week.
frus-1945-50-intel-d27:
Forrestal wrote to Secretary of State Byrnes on 13 October 1945, the same day he wrote to Secretary Patterson. The Navy secretary was working both channels of the argument at once. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Twin letters on one day show a man managing a two-front negotiation. To Patterson, Forrestal spoke as a partner; to Byrnes, as the head of a department with claims to press. Readers who pair the two letters can watch the same mind adjust its voice to its audience, a core skill of cabinet politics. The volume's gift is that it prints both sides of such days, letting the reader sit where only the writers once sat.
frus-1945-50-intel-d127:
Hoover wrote to Vandenberg, the director of central intelligence, on 19 August 1946. The two chiefs addressed each other directly after weeks of writing through others. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Direct letters between rivals late in a fight often carry terms: what each will do, and what each expects. Hoover and Vandenberg had circled each other through the attorney general, the authority, and the State Department. Their August exchange brought the dispute to the level where it would actually be lived, bureau to group, station by station. Readers can close the summer's story here, with the two men whose names stand for the era's two secret services facing each other on paper.
frus-1945-50-intel-d227:
On 10 October 1947, Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter sent a memorandum to the Intelligence Advisory Board. It survives in print as document 227 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d327:
A letter dated 29 October 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Acting Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The State Department prints it as document 327 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The shift from the old group to the CIA was fresh. The Council was still learning how to run its side of the work.

The letter form mattered in this world: it was signed, it was kept, and it bound the writer's office to what it said. Read in sequence, the letters show two offices testing how far each could push the other. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d427:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 7 came out on 12 February 1948. It is document 427 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

By early 1948 the first rule book was already growing. New directives filled gaps that the December 1947 set had left open. Each short order fixed one more duty, one more limit, or one more shared task. The series as a whole shows a state building its secret arm in plain, stepwise form. By February the agencies had real habits to codify, not just hopes on paper. The series can be read as a diary of the system's growth, one dated order at a time.
frus-1861-d27:
On 22 June 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to Henry Sanford in Brussels. The letter is document 27 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two letters in two days show a Secretary working his posts hard. The mails moved slowly, so Seward sent word whenever a point needed stress. Readers can feel the pace of a man trying to run a world wide effort from one desk in Washington. Paired days like this show Seward clearing the Brussels file in one focused sweep of the pen. One focused sweep of the pen could clear a week's Brussels business by noon.
frus-1861-d127:
William Dayton sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 June 1861. It is document 127 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

June opened with France still weighing its public stance on the war. Dayton's reports tracked each shade of that debate. His first of June letter adds one more careful reading from the post that watched Napoleon III most closely. France declared its neutrality in June, on terms close to those Britain had set. Terms close to Britain's made the two neutral walls a single front in law.
frus-1861-d227:
On 8 July 1861, Mr. Fogg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 227 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d27:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 6 March 1862. It stands as Document 27 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the winter of the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d127:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 13 August 1862. It stands as Document 127 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d227:
Two Seward letters to William Stuart are dated 20 August 1862, and the first stands as Document 227 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was the acting head of the British legation in Washington.

Paired letters on a single date usually divide topics so each can be answered and filed on its own. The practice is a window into how a paper government worked: neat, numbered, and slow. Late August 1862 was anything but slow on the battlefield. And the contrast between the calm file and the moving armies is part of what makes these papers vivid. Formal notes left a paper record that both governments could quote back to each other later.
frus-1862-d327:
William L. Dayton wrote from Paris on 17 September 1862, the day of Antietam, in a report printed as Document 327 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

The coincidence is the point: while the war's bloodiest day was fought in Maryland, the Union's man in Paris wrote in complete ignorance of it. His letter preserves the French scene as it stood before the news arrived. Few papers in the volume show the ocean's width, and diplomacy's blindness, more plainly than this one. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d427:
Horace J. Perry wrote from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 September 1862, four days after the battle of Antietam. The report is Document 427 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

News of Antietam and of Lincoln's coming emancipation order reached Europe slowly, and agents like Perry had to explain both to foreign courts. In Madrid the questions were sharp: would emancipation change Spain's view, and what would it mean for slavery in Cuba? Perry's September report fed Washington the Spanish reading of a turning point in the war. It belongs to the autumn file in which the Union's case abroad began to firm up.
frus-1862-d527:
The Washington exchange with the Netherlands minister opens on 5 June 1862, with Secretary of State William H. Seward writing to Roest van Limburg at his legation. The note is Document 527 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Van Limburg represented a government whose minister abroad, James Shepherd Pike, fills the Hague half of this same file. The first week of June 1862 brought a burst of Dutch business in Washington, with notes crossing almost daily. Seward's opening letter began that run. Resident ministers handled everything from trade complaints to questions of neutral right. The Dutch file that week shows how much formal paper a single matter could generate.
frus-1862-d627:
On 19 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Edward Joy Morris, the American minister to the Ottoman Empire. It is Document 627 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Seward wrote two days after Antietam, in the great mid-September round of orders, and even Constantinople was included. The news that followed, of emancipation declared, would reach the Bosphorus weeks later and be read there chiefly for its effect on the European powers. Morris's post stood at the edge of the war's diplomatic world, but Seward's system had no edges. Every minister got the line. He got it in the same week and in the same terms. The letter proves the system's reach.
frus-1863p1-d27:
On 8 January 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 27 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Paired dispatches let an envoy keep topics apart: one sheet for talks with officials, one for the press or the street. Adams wrote in that habit through the war. This letter is the second of his New Year pair's follow-up, sent as London digested the freedom edict. In the run of the file, it marks how fast the legation's mail could move when the news was big.
frus-1863p1-d127:
On 24 March 1863, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, and a second letter to him bears the same date. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 127 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Same-day pairs from Washington split the brief for clean use in London. Seward's late-March sheets kept Adams armed as the fight over Southern ships in British yards grew hot. This letter opens the pair of 24 March. With its mate, it shows the State Department feeding its envoy point by point, steamer by steamer, through a tense spring.
frus-1863p1-d227:
From his London post on 3 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 227 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

After the Emancipation Proclamation took effect on New Year's Day 1863, the war stood openly as a fight over slavery. That change made British support for the South harder to defend in public. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d327:
In Washington on 2 November 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 327 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d427:
In the flow of wartime mail, Lord Lyons wrote to William H. Seward on 27 March 1863. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d527:
The letter printed as document 527 was written on 22 May 1863 by William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d627:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote this official letter to Mr. Smith on 8 May 1863. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020327:
Cecile Martinat, Shoshana Shendelman, Alan Jonason, and their team built a Parkinson's cell model in PLOS Biology in 2004. A gene called DJ-1, when broken, causes a rare early form of Parkinson's disease. The team made dopamine neurons from stem cells that lack DJ-1 and stressed them with oxidants.

Those neurons died more readily than normal ones under the same stress. That result links DJ-1 to protection against oxidative damage, a long-suspected factor in Parkinson's. A stem-cell model that can be grown in a dish lets labs test protective drugs fast. The study is thus both a clue about the disease and a tool for hunting treatments.
plos-pbio-0020427:
Graham E. J. Rodwell, Rebecca Sonu, Jacob M. Zahn, and a large team profiled the aging kidney in PLOS Biology in 2004. They measured gene activity in human kidneys across adult ages. Aging organs change slowly, and the kidney's changes affect how well it filters blood and handles drugs.

Their profile shows a clear age signature: sets of genes that rise or fall steadily with age. Such a signature can act as a clock for organ health, more precise than years alone. It also points to the processes that drive kidney aging, like shifts in immune and metabolic genes. That gives researchers targets for keeping kidneys working longer.
plos-pone-0000027:
Colin A. Russell, Leslie A. Real, and David L. Smith modeled rabies spread in PLOS ONE in 2006. Rabies moves through wildlife like raccoons and foxes, and its front advances across the land in waves. Real landscapes are patchy, with rivers, towns, and forests that speed or slow the virus.

Their model asks how such patchiness changes where control works best. Barriers and vaccine zones placed with the land in mind can beat uniform plans. Rabies control is costly and long, so smarter placement matters. The work is a case study in spatial disease control, useful for other infections that spread across mixed terrain.
plos-pone-0000127:
Matthew R. E. Symonds, Neil J. Gemmell, Tamsin L. Braisher, and colleagues published this research-policy study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It compares the publication output of men and women scientists. The goal is a fair metric of research performance, one that does not bake in bias from career breaks or part-time work.

Raw paper counts can mislead when judging who performs well. The authors look at how gender gaps in output are measured and propose a less biased yardstick. The work speaks to hiring, funding, and promotion decisions across science, where a skewed metric can quietly hold back whole groups of researchers.
plos-pone-0000227:
Xuhua Xia, Huang Huang, Malisa Carullo, and colleagues published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Vertebrate mitochondrial genomes, the small DNA circles inside cells' power plants, run under tight size limits. The authors describe a conflict between translation initiation and elongation, starting and continuing protein production, inside these compact genomes.

In a cramped genome, signals for starting a gene can collide with the machinery reading the previous one. The authors analyze how that conflict plays out across vertebrates. The work explains odd features of mitochondrial gene layout and adds to the picture of how these ancient genomes are organized.
plos-pone-0000327:
Xinyan Lu, Chad A. Shaw, Ankita Patel, and colleagues published this clinical genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Chromosomal microarray analysis scans a patient's genome for missing or extra chunks too small for a microscope to see. The authors summarize the clinical implementation of the test across 2513 postnatal cases, children tested after birth for developmental problems.

A summary that large shows the test's real-world yield: how often it finds an answer. Microarrays were then becoming the first-line test for unexplained developmental delay. The paper documents that transition with numbers clinics could plan around.
plos-pone-0000427:
Massimo Buvoli, Ada Buvoli, and Leslie A. Leinwand studied how muscle cells handle faulty messages, using a mouse model of muscular dystrophy, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The mdx mouse carries a defect in the dystrophin gene. The team examined how exonic splicing enhancers, DNA-letter motifs that help splice a gene's message, interact with mRNA processing and mRNA surveillance.

Surveillance systems destroy garbled messages before they make harmful proteins, but they can also destroy messages the cell could have used. In a dystrophic muscle, that balance affects how much working protein the cell can salvage. The work speaks to therapies that coax cells to skip damaged exons and keep more of the message.
plos-pone-0000527:
Simona Ozden and colleagues showed that a mosquito-borne virus can infect human muscle's repair cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Chikungunya virus causes fever and severe joint pain, and its 2005–2006 outbreaks reached new regions. The team found that human muscle satellite cells, the stem cells that repair muscle, are targets of chikungunya virus infection.

Muscle pain and weakness are major features of the disease, yet the virus's targets in muscle were unclear. Infection of the repair crew itself could explain slow recovery: the cells needed for healing are under attack. The finding directs attention to muscle as a site where the virus may persist.
plos-pone-0000627:
Jason W. Locasale used computation to probe a short-term memory inside T cells, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. T cells are immune cells that meet antigen-presenting cells, which show them fragments of invaders. Recent studies had found that T cells can add up signals across interrupted meetings. The total behaves as if the cell remembers the earlier encounter.

Locasale built a simple mathematical model of that signal integration. The model hunts for the chemical steps that could hold a trace between meetings. A clear model gives experimentalists specific predictions to test in real cells. It also frames a general puzzle: how brief molecular events store information, even briefly.
plos-pone-0000727:
Laurence Fiévez, Christophe Desmet, Emmanuelle Henry and colleagues called a signaling protein a two-faced regulator of neutrophil balance, in PLOS ONE in 2007. STAT5 promotes the survival of the progenitor cells that make blood. Yet mice lacking STAT5 develop mild neutrophilia, an excess of neutrophils, the most common white blood cells. That paradox drives the study.

The authors show that in these mice, liver endothelial cells autonomously secrete large amounts of G-CSF, a growth factor for neutrophils. Progenitors then overcompensate for their own handicap. An ambivalent regulator indeed: STAT5 both supports blood cell survival and holds their numbers down through distant signals.
plos-pone-0000827:
Veronika Hartmannsgruber, Willm-Thomas Heyken, Michael Kacik and colleagues showed that arteries' answer to blood flow hinges on one channel protein. In blood vessels, the endothelium is the inner lining. It is a key signal interface that controls vessel tone and blood pressure. That control ensures energy and oxygen supply matches organs' needs. The lining answers vasoactive factors and the shear stress of flowing blood.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE title states the critical dependence: the arterial response to shear stress depends on endothelial TRPV4 expression. TRPV4 is a channel that senses mechanical and chemical cues. A single channel carrying the flow signal makes it a candidate lever for blood pressure control.
plos-pone-0000927:
John Azevedo, Emily Tietz, Tashena Two-Feathers and colleagues compared how cyclists burned the sugars in two sports drinks, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Riders took either a drink with lactate polymer, fructose and glucose, or a leading rival drink built on fructose. Six male cyclists in the top amateur classes rode through steady exercise while the team measured fuel use.

The question was practical: which mix of sugars actually gets burned during hard effort. Drinks often promise more than the body can use. Measuring oxidation profiles, how each sugar is taken up and burned, gives riders and makers real numbers. Small trials like this keep sports claims honest.
plos-pone-0001027:
Marta Szulkin and Ben Sheldon studied how the cost of inbreeding shifts with conditions in wild birds, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inbreeding depression is the fitness loss in offspring of relatives. It is usually blamed on harmful recessive gene copies showing themselves when inherited from both parents.

The open question is how much that loss depends on the environment. Hard years might expose inbred young more than easy ones. A wild bird population gives the test real setting: pedigrees, weather and survival all recorded. The answer matters for small populations, where inbreeding is forced and managers must know when it hurts most.
plos-pone-0001127:
Head lice are usually treated with insecticide liquids, but there were signs the standard drug was losing its punch. Ian Burgess, Peter Lee, and Geraldine Matlock ran a clinical trial, reported in 2007 in PLOS ONE, comparing two treatments. One was 4 percent dimeticone lotion. The other was 0.5 percent malathion liquid, the most prescribed head louse treatment in the United Kingdom for about ten years.

The trial was randomized and controlled, and the people judging results did not know which treatment each patient got. Anecdotal reports had suggested malathion worked less well than before, but that had not been confirmed in a clinic. The study put both options to a fair head-to-head test.
plos-pone-0001227:
The axolotl, a Mexican salamander, can regrow a whole limb perfectly after amputation, something no mammal can do. Mathieu Lévesque and colleagues asked which signals that regrowth requires, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The axolotl limb is the most widely used model for studying vertebrate regeneration.

The authors report that signaling by transforming growth factor beta is essential for limb regeneration in axolotls. Block the signal, and the celebrated regrowth fails. Knowing a required signal in an animal that regenerates is a clue for the much harder question of why mammals mostly cannot.
plos-pone-0001327:
Some neurons do not fire spikes; the retinal rod bipolar cell is one. Lorenzo Cangiano and colleagues studied how such a cell filters its inputs, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. These cells carry the eye's signals for dim light, mediated by a current called Ih, which flows through HCN channels.

In spiking neurons, Ih mostly supports rhythmic activity. The authors report high-pass filtering of input signals by the Ih current in the rod bipolar cell: slow signals are damped, faster ones pass. That filtering shapes what the retina tells the brain about changing light.
